extracted.intended_audience: employers, labor attorneys, small businesses, policymakers, researchers, and other stakeholders engaged in DOL rulemaking or worker-classification analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Final-rule guidance and analytic standards for determining whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor under the FLSA, together with the Department's economic impact analysis (including RFA analysis) and consideration of regulatory alternatives. Includes descriptions of the multifactor economic reality test and the methods used to estimate costs, transfers, and impacts on small entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality-of-the-circumstances economic reality test
rubrics_metrics.description: Return to a totality-of-the-circumstances analysis of the economic reality test in which the factors do not have a predetermined weight and are considered in view of the economic reality of the whole activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule does not use 'core factors' and instead assesses all relevant facts together; factors are not assigned preset importance. The Department believes this approach more fully reflects case law and is relevant to the evolving economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment factor (separate factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Investment is framed as a separate factor and as an integral part of the potential employer's business rather than an integrated unit of production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule returns to longstanding framing of investment; the Department adjusted proposed regulatory text regarding the investment factor after considering comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control factor (including scheduling, supervision, price setting, ability to work for others, reserved rights, compliance obligations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Control factor should consider scheduling, remote supervision, price setting, the worker's ability to work for others, and reserved rights; it also addresses compliance with legal obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule provides broader discussion of how these elements should be considered under the control factor, and removes prior provisions that minimized the relevance of retained rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanency/exclusivity factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusivity is considered in the context of the permanency factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule discusses exclusivity as it relates to permanency of the relationship rather than treating exclusivity as dispositive on its own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill/initiative factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Initiative should be evaluated in the context of the skill factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule clarifies how initiative (e.g., marketing one's services, hiring helpers) relates to the worker's skill and autonomy when assessing economic dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of 'core factors' approach
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulations do not use 'core factors' or assign predetermined weights to factors when determining status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach is intended to avoid narrowing the economic reality test and to ensure relevant facts are not excluded by an artificial weighting scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of reserved/retained rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Reserved rights of the potential employer may be considered under the control factor and should not be minimized automatically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule allows consideration of reserved rights (even if not exercised) in evaluating control, while removing prior provisions that minimized their relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of preamble and notice-and-comment for authoritative guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Issuing regulations with an explanatory preamble and using the notice-and-comment process provides in-depth guidance and allows courts to consider agency regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department chose to issue regulations rather than rely only on subregulatory guidance because formal rulemaking permits collection of stakeholder views and potentially improves judicial consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory alternatives assessment (Executive Order 12866)
rubrics_metrics.description: As required by Executive Order 12866, the Department must assess regulatory alternatives, including consideration of legal constraints, benefits, costs, and impacts, and explain why alternatives were accepted or rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department assessed four alternatives (including common-law or ABC tests, partial retention of the 2021 IC Rule, rescission without replacement via subregulatory guidance, and rescind-and-replace with multifactor regulations) and explained why complete rescission and replacement was chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Familiarization Cost Estimation
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate time and wage rates for stakeholders to familiarize themselves with the rule (Department increased estimate to 1 hour for firms and 30 minutes for independent contractors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department used the Compensation, Benefits, and Job Analysis Specialist occupation wage consistent with prior rules; explanatory text notes some commenters argued higher-paid staff would review, but the Department used a consistent occupation and adjusted the time estimate to represent an average.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish transfers from costs in economic analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain impacts (e.g., employer-provided benefits shifting to workers) are treated as transfers rather than net social costs in the economic analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: costs of health insurance or retirement benefits are considered transfers and discussed in a separate section of the economic analysis (section VII.E). The Department explains that transfers (changes in who bears costs/benefits) differ from regulatory compliance costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include employer-provided fringe benefits valuation
rubrics_metrics.description: When estimating transfers from reclassification, calculate the value of employer-provided health insurance, retirement, and paid leave using BLS Employer Costs for Employee Compensation applied to median wages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department used BLS series to compute benefit share (%) and applied to median weekly wages (inflated using GDP Deflator) to estimate annual value (e.g., estimated average > $15,000 for full-time independent contractors). The estimate may be reduced if wages adjust downward to offset employer costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider tax liability shifts (FICA and state revenues)
rubrics_metrics.description: In converting workers from independent contractors to employees, account for shifts in payroll tax liabilities (e.g., employer FICA components) and potential impacts on state tax revenue and program funding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department noted independent contractors currently pay both employee and employer shares of FICA; reclassification could transfer some tax liabilities to employers and affect state unemployment insurance, workers' compensation funds, and other programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider FLSA protections and wage/overtime impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze how reduced misclassification affects applicability of minimum wage, overtime pay, and other FLSA protections and estimate potential transfers related to unpaid minimum wage/overtime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use CWS data to compare incidence of wages below minimum and overtime work between independent contractors and employees; account for how reclassification could increase hourly wages and overtime pay where misclassification previously denied protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess prevalence and harms of misclassification (distributional impacts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider evidence on prevalence of misclassification (e.g., studies showing 10–30% misclassification in audits) and the disproportionate effects on BIPOC workers and certain industries (construction, trucking, home care, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use literature, state audits, and sector-specific studies to inform expected benefits of the rule in reducing misclassification and impacts on underserved groups; commenters provided studies and industry-specific estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic methodology for wage comparisons (regression approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: To compare earnings of independent contractors and employees, regress hourly wages on independent contractor status and observable covariates (occupation, sex, experience, education, race/ethnicity) to isolate the effect of status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department followed an approach similar to Katz and Krueger (2018) using the 2017 CWS and also ran regressions with interaction terms for female, Hispanic, and Black independent contractors to examine heterogeneous effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: RFA requirements: assess impacts on small entities and consider alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Regulatory Flexibility Act, agencies must consider the impact of rules on small businesses, non-profits, and small governmental jurisdictions, identify whether the rule would have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities, consider alternatives to minimize impact, and solicit public comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final regulatory flexibility analysis (FRFA) describes need for rulemaking, objectives, and summarizes significant issues raised in public comments, including SBA Office of Advocacy concerns; it responds to comments about underestimating impacts and explains why the Department does not view compliance with law as a 'cost' for purposes of the economic analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of commenters' claims about additional costs (reclassification, lost work, disruptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Document and respond to stakeholder claims that the Department failed to estimate costs for reclassification, lost work, business disruptions, payroll tax obligations, benefits, and increased compensation demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains its view that the rule will not lead to widespread reclassification and provides qualitative discussion of potential transfers; it adjusted familiarization estimates in response to comments and explains why some claims were not quantified as net costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: SBREFA/enforcement accommodations concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider commenters' requests for exemptions or penalty-waiver accommodations for small entities (asserting that small businesses may misapply the economic reality test and deserve reduced penalties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters asked for waivers or reduced penalties under SBREFA; the Department addresses these concerns in the FRFA and related discussion of enforcement and small-entity impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior rule comparisons and judicial precedent consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: When crafting a new regulation, compare it to prior departmental rules (e.g., 2021 IC Rule) and ensure consistency with longstanding judicial precedent and Department guidance prior to the prior rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains where the 2021 IC Rule narrowed the economic reality test in ways inconsistent with case law and why a rescission-and-replace approach better aligns with precedent; it cites courts' use of agency regulations when considering classification issues.
